title: Hail, full of grace (Luke 1:26–38)
hookLine: the angel's greeting, Mary's question, and her yes

lines: AND THE VIRGIN'S NAME WAS MARY.
cards: Six months later, Luke says, the same angel is sent again. But look where. Last time, the sanctuary of the Temple in Jerusalem, and a priest at the altar of incense.
This time, a town in Galilee called Nazareth, and a young woman espoused to a man named Joseph, of the house of David. No altar. No incense.
No crowd outside. Luke gives her name last, as if he's saving it: and the virgin's name was Mary.

teach.b: The angel comes in and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." Hail, in Latin, is Ave.
The Greek word, chaire, was an ordinary greeting that also means rejoice.
Full of grace translates one Greek word, kecharitomene, a form meaning something like one who has been graced, and remains so. It's the angel's name for her, almost in place of her name.
Catholics hear in it the fullness of grace that marks Mary's whole life; the King James has highly favored. Mary is troubled, and wonders what kind of greeting this is.
Fear not, the angel says, you have found grace with God; you'll conceive and bear a son, and call him Jesus.
Then Mary asks a question, as Zachary did: "How shall this be done, because I know not man?" But it's a different question. Zachary asked how he could know.

Mary asks how it will happen. Some readers notice the difference: one asks for proof, the other for the way. The angel answers: the Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the most High shall overshadow thee.
Your kinswoman Elizabeth, the barren one, is in her sixth month, because no word shall be impossible with God.

teach.h: FIAT: BE IT DONE TO ME.
teach.b: Then her answer: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word."
In Latin, fiat: let it be. The angel departs. Catholics keep this moment as the feast of the Annunciation.

how: Catholics pray the Hail Mary, whose first half is the angel's greeting and Elizabeth's, in the rosary and the Angelus, and celebrate the Annunciation on March 25; the scene is the first Joyful Mystery of the rosary.

o: Latin for holy, a word for the saints
Latin for bird, a sign of the Spirit
Latin for hail, the angel's greeting

s: Mary asked for a sign the way Zachary did
Zachary asked how he could know; Mary asked how it would be done. some readers have noted the difference.
the first half of the Hail Mary comes from Luke's Gospel
the angel's greeting (1:28) and Elizabeth's words (1:42), with the names added.
Gabriel went to Mary in the Temple in Jerusalem
he went to Nazareth, a town in Galilee.

games.q: you're Mary in Nazareth. an angel says you will bear a son, though you know not man. what do you say?
o: ask how it will be done, and then say: be it done to me according to thy word.
games.why: she asks how, hears the answer, and says: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word."

practice: The first half of the Hail Mary is made of Luke's words, with two names added: the angel's greeting, and a few verses on, Elizabeth's.
If you pray, say it slowly, one phrase to each breath: Hail Mary, full of grace; the Lord is with thee; blessed art thou among women; and blessed is the fruit of thy womb, Jesus.
If you don't pray it, sit with the greeting itself, the Lord is with thee, and notice what it would be like to hear it said to you.

wordCard.voice: Ave. Latin for hail, the angel Gabriel's first word to Mary at Nazareth, and the first word of the Hail Mary. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: full of grace, highly favored; a form meaning one who has been graced, and remains so.

carryVoice: Your line: full of grace. She asked how, then said yes. That's day four hundred forty-four.
